subject: US core CPI ran hot. Canadian fixed rates feel it
bodyMarkdown:
The US inflation report that landed Friday morning made a Federal Reserve rate hike on Wednesday the market's base case, and the reason I care about it from Richmond Hill is that the same repricing runs through the bond yield that sets five-year fixed mortgage rates here. Nobody in Washington votes on your renewal letter, and it reaches there anyway.

## What Friday's number said

CNBC reported on Friday that the US consumer price index rose 0.4 per cent in August, putting the annual rate at 3.4 per cent. The line that moved money was **core CPI**, which strips out food and energy so you can see the underlying trend instead of a gasoline spike, and it rose 0.3 per cent on the month against the 0.2 per cent forecasters expected, the fastest since April. The annual core rate ticked down to 2.4 per cent from 2.5, which tells you how much of the problem is energy and how much is everything else. Airline fares jumped 2.7 per cent as jet fuel got dearer. Traders did not read any of it as noise. Trading Economics data put the US 10-year Treasury yield near 4.97 per cent on Friday, its highest since October 2023.

## Why Wednesday is live

The Fed's target range is 3.50 to 3.75 per cent and the FOMC meets Tuesday and Wednesday. Reuters reported on Friday that the implied odds of a quarter-point hike next week rose to 71 per cent after the CPI release. That is an odd sentence to write in 2026, when the argument a year ago was about how many cuts were left. Kevin Warsh changed it. CNBC reported on August 28 that the chair told his Jackson Hole audience the central bank still has "work to do" on inflation, and two-year yields jumped the same day. My read is that a hike on Wednesday is now the cheaper choice for him. He has spent a month saying he is uncomfortable, and standing pat after a hot core print would cost more credibility than a quarter point costs the economy.

## The part that lands on a mortgage here

Reuters reported on Friday that the loonie slipped to 1.3862 per US dollar, or 72.14 US cents, its weakest level since September 2. A wider rate gap does that, and a softer loonie makes imported goods dearer. Canadian yields also track American ones more closely than the Bank of Canada would like. The five-year Government of Canada yield has been running near 3.3 per cent, close to a 12-month high, and Ratehub listed the best five-year fixed mortgage rate at 4.09 per cent on Thursday. The Bank held at 2.25 per cent on September 2 for a seventh straight decision, and CBC reported that day that Tiff Macklem called July inflation of 3 per cent too high for comfort. Canada lost 42,000 jobs in August, per Statistics Canada, and unemployment sits at 6.4 per cent. That is a weak labour market paying for somebody else's inflation fight.

## The takeaway

Canada's August inflation report comes out Monday morning, and after Friday I will look at the core measures the Bank of Canada targets before I look at the headline. If you are renewing a mortgage inside the next six months, take a rate hold now, since lenders will hold a quote for up to 120 days and it costs you nothing if rates fall instead. Reuters reported on September 2 that money markets were already pricing a quarter-point Bank of Canada increase by December and about three more next year. The Fed announces on Wednesday afternoon.
